# The situation

An integrated species distribution model fuses data sources with different
sampling protocols: a large, messy, presence-only arm (GBIF, eBird) and a
smaller, structured survey arm (a monitoring programme). The whole design
rests on the two arms measuring the same underlying process, so that the
structured arm can discipline the biased one.

They usually differ in one respect nobody puts in the model. **The
presence-only arm knows where it is; the survey arm often does not.**

This is not sloppiness — it is policy. Monitoring programmes routinely
publish coordinates degraded on purpose, to protect site access agreements
and to avoid disclosing the locations of species at risk. The Alberta
Biodiversity Monitoring Institute publishes public survey locations
**fuzzed to roughly 5.5 km**, and coarser still for sensitive species;
precise coordinates require a separate data agreement. Meanwhile an eBird
checklist in the same landscape carries a GPS fix.

So the two arms are fused as though both located their observations equally
well, and one of them did not.

# Why this is easy to wave away

The intuition that makes this feel harmless goes: *the model has a spatial
random field; positional error is spatial noise; the field will absorb it.*

That intuition is about the **response**. The damage is to the
**covariate**.

Environmental predictors in an SDM are almost never measured at the site.
They are extracted from a raster at the recorded coordinate. If the recorded
coordinate is wrong by 5.5 km, you read temperature, elevation, or canopy
cover **from the wrong place** — and you then regress the species' response,
which happened at the *true* location, on the covariate value from a
different one.

That is textbook errors-in-variables. Its signature is **attenuation**: the
estimated slope is biased toward zero. And it lands on exactly the quantity
an SDM exists to produce — the environmental response curve.

How bad it is depends on one ratio: the positional error relative to the
**correlation length of the environment**, not its size in kilometres. Fuzz
of 5.5 km is nearly harmless across a smooth continental temperature
gradient and severe across a patchy canopy-cover layer.

# Measuring it

The claim above is checkable, so it should be checked rather than asserted.

The simulation is in `dev/isdm-precision/precision-sim.R`. Both arms observe
the same landscape and the same truth: counts are generated from the
environment at each site's **true** location, with a shared slope
$\beta = 0.9$. The arms differ in one respect only — the presence-only arm
records its coordinates exactly, and the survey arm's recorded coordinates
are displaced by Gaussian noise with standard deviation `fuzz` × the
environmental correlation length. The covariate handed to the model is read
at each arm's *recorded* location, which is what an analyst would do.

Three analyses of the identical world:

- **`precise_only`** — fit the presence-only arm alone.
- **`fuzzed_only`** — fit the survey arm alone.
- **`integrated`** — fit both together, the thing an iSDM actually does.

40 replicates at each of four fuzz levels.

# What happens

Mean estimated slope (true value **0.9**), with attenuation as a percentage
of truth:

| fuzz (× corr. length) | `precise_only` | `fuzzed_only` | `integrated` |
|---|---|---|---|
| **0.00** | 0.895 (0.6%) | 0.910 (−1.2%) | 0.902 (−0.2%) |
| **0.25** | 0.902 (−0.2%) | 0.579 (**35.7%**) | 0.741 (**17.6%**) |
| **0.50** | 0.907 (−0.8%) | 0.403 (**55.2%**) | 0.652 (**27.6%**) |
| **1.00** | 0.902 (−0.2%) | 0.216 (**76.0%**) | 0.545 (**39.4%**) |

Three things to read off it.

**The control works.** At `fuzz = 0` all three analyses agree on 0.90. Whatever
the integration machinery does, it is not the source of the bias — the bias
appears only when positional error does.

**The precise arm is untouched.** Across every row it sits at 0.895–0.907,
bias under 0.01. Adding fuzz to the *other* arm cannot hurt it, which is
what makes the last column so awkward.

**Attenuation is severe and it survives integration.** At displacement equal
to the environmental correlation length the fuzzed arm retains less than a
quarter of the true slope. Integration dilutes that damage — 39.4% rather
than 76.0% — but does not remove it. The structured arm does not get
disciplined by the precise one; it drags the precise one down.

# The uncomfortable part

Compare the first and last columns.

At every non-zero fuzz level, **the integrated estimate is further from the
truth than the presence-only arm alone**. At `fuzz = 0.5`, discarding the
survey data entirely gives 0.907 against a true 0.9; fusing it gives 0.652.

That inverts the premise of the method. Integrated SDMs are motivated by the
structured arm correcting the opportunistic one. Here the structured arm
carries a defect the opportunistic arm does not have, and integration
propagates it — so more data yields a worse answer, with narrower intervals
around it, because the model has no way to know that one arm's covariates
are mismeasured.

None of this is an argument against integrated SDMs. It is an argument that
**positional precision belongs in the list of things you check before fusing
two sources**, alongside detection probability and sampling effort — and it
currently is not on that list.

# What to do about it

`gllvmTMB` does not implement a fix, and this article does not claim one.
What the measurement supports:

1. **Check the ratio before fusing.** Compare each arm's positional
   uncertainty to the correlation length of your covariates — a variogram
   on the raster, not a glance at the map. Fuzz well below the correlation
   length is benign; the table above starts biting around a quarter of it.
2. **Fit the arms separately first.** If the precise-arm-alone and
   integrated slopes disagree materially, that gap is evidence, not noise.
   It is cheap and it is the diagnostic the table above is built on.
3. **Aggregate to the fuzz scale.** If survey coordinates are fuzzed to
   5.5 km, covariates extracted at 5.5 km resolution are read at
   approximately the right place; a 30 m raster read at a fuzzed coordinate
   is not. Matching covariate resolution to positional precision is the
   cheapest available mitigation, and it costs the fine-scale signal.
4. **Ask for the precise coordinates.** Most fuzzing regimes, ABMI's
   included, have a data-agreement route to exact locations. For an analysis
   that turns on an environmental slope, that request is worth making before
   the analysis rather than after.

The general fix — an errors-in-variables layer with a per-arm positional
prior — is a real modelling option and is not implemented here. Treat this
article as a reason to measure your own case, not as a solution to it.

# Scope and limits

Stated plainly, because the table is more persuasive than the evidence
behind it warrants if these are omitted:

- **Simulation only.** No real ABMI or GBIF data was fitted here. The 5.5 km
  figure is documented ABMI policy and motivates the design; it is not a
  measurement of bias in any real dataset.
- **One error model.** Isotropic Gaussian displacement. Administrative
  fuzzing is often uniform-within-a-cell or grid-snapped, which will not
  behave identically.
- **One covariate structure.** A single smooth exponential-correlation
  surface. Patchier or anisotropic covariates will attenuate differently,
  and the fuzz-to-correlation-length ratio is the axis that matters.
- **Fixed effects only.** No latent field is fitted, so this isolates the
  covariate channel. Positional error also corrupts the estimated spatial
  field; that is not measured here.
- **No coverage claim.** Point estimates only. Whether intervals around
  these attenuated slopes retain nominal coverage is a separate question and
  is not answered.
